lines.t: Excuse me, do you know if the bookstore is still open?
I'm sorry I missed your presentation. How did it go?
Would you mind closing the window? It's getting a little cold in here.
I was hoping to switch into your lab section, but it looks like it's full.
Do you mind if I borrow your notes from Tuesday's class?
I can't believe the workshop got cancelled again.
Hi Kenji, come in. What can I do for you?
Hi. I'm thinking about dropping my statistics course, and I wanted to ask whether that's still possible this late in the term.
Well, the deadline to withdraw without a penalty is this Friday. After that, a W appears on your transcript.
Oh, I thought it had already passed. Good. The thing is, the class is much faster than I expected, and I'm also working twelve hours a week at the bookstore.
I see. Have you talked to the professor, or been to the tutoring center?
I've been to the tutoring center twice, but the sessions are always full, and I can't get an appointment on the days I'm free.
Hmm. Before you drop, remember that statistics is required for your major. If you withdraw now, you'd have to take it next fall, which could delay your graduation by a semester.
I hadn't thought about that. Is there another option?
You could ask the professor for a study group list. She often pairs students up. And the department offers free evening workshops on Wednesdays, which don't need an appointment.
Wednesday evenings work for me. Maybe I should try that first and decide on Thursday.
That sounds sensible. Just remember, the form must reach my office by five o'clock on Friday.

Attention, residents of Fenwick Hall. Starting next Monday, the laundry room on the ground floor will close for repairs. It will reopen on the fourteenth. During this time, you may use the machines in Calder Hall, the building next to the dining center. Calder's laundry room is open from seven a.m. to eleven p.m., and it accepts the same ID cards. If you have a load already inside a machine, please collect it by Sunday night, because staff will remove anything left behind on Monday morning. Questions can be sent to the housing office.

Today I want to talk about one of the most remarkable skills in the animal world: how octopuses change their appearance. An octopus can match the color and even the texture of a rock or a patch of seaweed in less than a second. How? The answer lies in its skin. Embedded in the skin are thousands of tiny organs called chromatophores. Each one is a small sac of pigment surrounded by muscles. When the muscles pull, the sac stretches out and the color becomes visible. When they relax, the sac shrinks to a dot, and the color seems to vanish. Now, here's what surprises people. Octopuses are colorblind, at least as far as we can tell. Their eyes contain just one type of light-sensitive cell. So how do they match colors they cannot see? One idea is that the skin itself contains light-sensitive proteins, which let it detect brightness without the help of the eyes. Another idea is that the octopus uses the shape of its pupil to compare light from different angles. Researchers have not settled the question. What we do know is that camouflage is not only for hiding. Octopuses also flash bright patterns to startle predators, and males sometimes display bold stripes to attract mates. So the same system serves several purposes. For next week, please read the article on cephalopod vision, and think about which of the two explanations seems more convincing.

Let's turn to a tool that archaeologists rely on, though it doesn't look like a tool at all: pollen. Every flowering plant releases pollen, and its outer shell is incredibly durable. In wet soil, such as the bottom of a lake or a bog, pollen can survive for thousands of years. Layers of sediment build up over time, so by taking a long core of mud and counting the pollen grains in each layer, researchers can reconstruct which plants grew in an area, and when. Suppose a core shows oak and elm pollen for a long stretch, and then the oak suddenly drops while grass and cereal pollen rise. That pattern usually signals that people cleared the forest to plant crops. Now, there's a limitation. Pollen from some plants, like pine, travels for miles in the wind, so finding pine pollen doesn't prove that pines grew nearby. And insect-pollinated plants release much less pollen, so they may be underrepresented. That's why researchers combine pollen data with other evidence, such as seeds and charcoal, before drawing conclusions.

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, a pattern known as the urban heat island effect. Two main factors cause it. First, materials such as asphalt, brick and concrete absorb sunlight during the day and release the stored heat slowly at night, so cities cool down far less after sunset than fields do. Second, cities contain fewer plants. Vegetation cools the air through transpiration, the process by which plants release water vapor, and trees also provide shade. When forests and grassland are replaced with buildings and roads, this natural cooling is lost.

Heat islands have practical consequences. They raise demand for electricity as residents run air conditioners, and they can make heat waves more dangerous, especially for elderly people. Planners have tested several remedies. Painting roofs white reflects more sunlight, and planting trees along streets adds shade. Some cities have also created green roofs, which are rooftops covered with soil and plants. Studies suggest these measures can lower local temperatures by one to three degrees, although they are costly to install across an entire city.

items.q: According to the passage, why do cities cool down slowly after sunset?
options: Fields reflect heat back to the city
Their buildings release stored heat gradually

options: The release of water vapor by plants

items.q: Which of the following is NOT mentioned as a consequence of heat islands?
Why does the author mention green roofs?
options: To show that rooftops cannot be changed
To explain why cities are warmer

To give an example of a remedy planners have tried

items.q: What can be inferred about applying these remedies across a whole city?
options: It would cause temperatures to rise
It has no effect on temperature

tasks.title: Read an Academic Passage
tasks.text:
Every year, a tree adds a new layer of wood beneath its bark, and in many climates the layer is visible as a ring. In a wet year the ring is wide; in a dry or cold year it is narrow. Because trees of the same species in the same region respond to the same weather, their ring patterns match. Scientists called dendrochronologists exploit this fact. By overlapping the patterns of living trees with those of old timber from buildings, they can build a continuous record that stretches back thousands of years, a method known as crossdating. Once such a record exists, a beam of unknown age can be dated simply by matching its rings against the master sequence.

The technique has been used to date medieval churches and to settle disputes about when ancient settlements were abandoned. It has limits, however. Trees in tropical regions often lack distinct rings, because growth is nearly constant throughout the year. And a single tree may be missing a ring entirely in an extremely harsh year, which is why researchers never rely on one specimen alone. Instead, they compare dozens, using the group pattern to detect errors.

items.q: Why do the ring patterns of different trees in one region match?
options: The trees grow in old buildings
The trees are all the same age
The trees experience the same weather
The trees are measured by the same scientists

items.q: The word 'exploit' in the passage is closest in meaning to
Why do researchers compare dozens of specimens?
options: To reduce the cost of dating
To prove that tropical trees have rings
To detect rings that a single tree may be missing

items.q: What can be inferred about dating tropical timber with this method?
options: It would be difficult because rings are not distinct
It would be easier than in cold regions
It is the only method scientists use

email.title: Write an Email
email.prompt:
You are taking a biology course at a university. You missed last Thursday's lab session because you were sick, and the lab report is due next Monday.

Write an email to your professor, Dr. Hollis. In your email, do the following:
- Explain why you missed the lab.
- Ask whether you can make up the lab session or get the data from it.
- Ask whether the due date for the report can be moved.
email.subject: Missed lab on Thursday
email.rubric: Task: academic email to a professor. Must cover all 3 bullets. Look for appropriate register (polite, formal-neutral), greeting and sign-off, clear organization, accurate grammar, natural phrasing. Typical strong length 90-150 words.

discussion.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
discussion.prompt: Your professor is teaching a class on education. Post a reply to the professor's question. In your reply, state your view with a reason, and add something new to the thread. Aim for at least 100 words.

professor.name: Dr. Okafor
professor.text: This week we are discussing how schools should prepare students for work. Some people say schools should spend more time on practical skills such as budgeting, cooking and computer repair, even if this means fewer hours on traditional subjects like history or literature. Others say traditional subjects teach students how to think and should stay the priority. Which approach do you think is better, and why?

students.name: Kelly
students.text: I think practical skills should come first. Many graduates do not know how to manage money or sign a rental contract. Schools can still teach history, but a few hours a week of real-life skills would help everyone.

students.name: Andre
students.text: I disagree. Practical skills change quickly, but the ability to read carefully and argue clearly never goes out of date. Students can learn budgeting from their families or online, but not critical thinking.

discussion.rubric: Task: academic discussion post, 100+ words. Look for a clear opinion, specific support or examples, engagement with at least one classmate's point (not just repeating), coherence, varied accurate grammar and vocabulary.
